items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: I had groupies, I had American groupies, and they would come … you know, this was a Japanese club so Americans are not supposed to be there. So I had these groupies, about four of them, they were in the backstage and listening. And this club, downstairs there was a coffee shop, Japanese coffee shops are usually restaurants. Every once in a while the MPs would come. So MPs would come, and they would go

downstairs [laughs]. So they were the groupies. One of the groupies, his nickname … we used to call him “Mac,” because his whole full name was McCutchen—I don‟t quite remember the first name [Harry], but McCutchen—and he was an Air Force sergeant or something and he was a jazz fan and one of the groupies. And he told me about Oscar Pettiford‟s group, and that he would take me to backstage. And he took me to backstage and I saw … this was the first time in my life I saw people warming up. You know, I‟d never seen…
J.J. didn‟t explain why Miles wasn‟t working? Did he give any indication why?

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: And Charlie Rice, the drummer, I forgot the name of the guitar player

ctx.x: Yes. The first great pianist I had met actually in person was Oscar Peterson. That was in 1953 I believe. That was the first time the American jazz group came to Japan for the Japanese audience. Before that a few groups came to Japan but they were for the USO

tour for the American troops. For example, Louis Armstrong was there one time, and the Gene Krupa Trio was there one time, and way before that, in 1950 I believe there was a dance band, Les Brown’s band with Bob Hope. But more than anything, I think ’51, I’m not quite sure, there is Oscar Pettiford the leader, and J.J. Johnson and Howard McGhee, they were also on the USO tour. And Charlie Rice, the drummer, I forgot the name of the guitar player, they didn’t have a pianist for the USO tour, because the piano you…
